questions.question_text: Among the following, which is considered to be the most significant therapeutic factor in group psychotherapy?

options.text: Expression of emotion and cathartic release of tensions

questions.explanation: Cohesion is the sense that the group is working together towards a common goal. This is believed to be the most important factor related to positive therapeutic effects. Group cohesion has been likened to the therapeutic alliance in dyadic treatment. In dynamic therapies, specifi c and non-specifi c elements contribute to therapeutic change. In groups, the presence of other people adds to factors present in all dyadic healing relationships. Non-specifi c factors are embedded in the relationships established through a consistent, accepting, non-judgemental, and supportive environment. These are all elements of a cohesive group. Groups provide a corrective emotional experience in which patients experience others (including the therapist) responding to them differently from those in their past. Members share their stories (catharsis) and feel less isolated when others have shared similar stories (universalization); they have opportunities to be helpful to others through both cognitive understanding and emotional linking (imparting information, providing feedback, and altruism). They also see others improve, which conveys hope. These elements contribute to the sense of collaboration and a willingness to adopt norms (i.e. discuss feelings about the interactions in the meeting) that further members’ sense of effi cacy and belonging. They contribute to an experience of support and acceptance, which may be suffi cient therapeutic gain for a number of patients. Fight/fl ight, pairing, and dependency are Bion’s basic group assumptions that lead to a negative therapeutic effect. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2007, p. 1908.

questions.question_text: Covert sensitisation is best used in the treatment of which of the following

options.text: A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder
A diagnosis of major depressive disorder

questions.explanation: Covert sensitisation is a variant of aversive conditioning wherein images (e.g. of drinking situations) is paired with imaginary aversive stimuli (e.g. a scene of a person vomiting all over the place, or a scene of a person dying of alcohol-induced liver damage). It is called covert because neither the undesirable stimulus nor the aversive stimulus is actually presented except in the imagination. Sensitization refers to the intention to build up an avoidance response to the undesirable stimulus. This is based on aversion therapy. Freeman C and Power M. Handbook of Evidence-based Psychotherapies: A Guide for Research and Practice, 1st edn. WileyBlackwell, 2007, p. 70.

questions.question_text: According to Freud's structural model, the ego functions primarily as which of the following?

options.text: The source of instinctual and sexual impulses
The seat of internalised moral values and conscience
The executive organ of the mind linked with reality
The unconscious repository of repressed conflicts
The mediator between the individual's fantasies and internal desires

correct_answer.text: The executive organ of the mind linked with reality

questions.explanation: The ego is explicitly described as the executive organ of the mind linked with reality. Option A describes the id. Option B describes the superego. Option D describes the unconscious aspects of the id. Option E, while partially related to the ego's function, is less precise than the definition of it as the executive organ.

questions.question_text: In psychoanalytic theory, which instinctual force is associated with Thanatos?
questions.explanation: Thanatos is specifically defined as the Death instinct encompassing destructive and aggressive instincts. Eros is the Life instinct encompassing life-affirming libidinal and sexual instincts. The pressure from instincts seeking fulfillment leads to anxiety.

questions.question_text: Parapraxes, or Freudian slips, are understood in psychoanalytic theory as resulting from which mechanism?

options.text: Conscious deliberate mimicry of others' speech
Return of repressed materials that slip out as words during conversation
Displacement of anxiety onto speech patterns

correct_answer.text: Return of repressed materials that slip out as words during conversation

questions.explanation: Parapraxes are specifically understood as due to the return of the repressed materials that slip out as words during conversation, giving clues to what is in the unconscious. This reflects the dynamic return of repressed content rather than neurological deficit or other mechanisms.

questions.question_text: Melanie Klein's concept of the depressive position involves which developmental achievement?

options.text: Fear of retaliation from the bad object
Retreat and cutting off from others
Integration of good and bad aspects and development of guilt and wish to repair
Formation of the superego through identification

correct_answer.text: Integration of good and bad aspects and development of guilt and wish to repair

questions.explanation: The depressive position is specifically described as occurring once an infant can integrate good and bad qualities in the mother (seeing her as having both), leading to feelings of guilt and a wish to repair any damage caused. This represents developmental progress from the paranoid-schizoid position's splitting.

questions.question_text: In dynamic psychotherapy, the therapist at times uses certain techniques that represent the ‘supportive’ end of the psychodynamic continuum rather than the ‘expressive’ end. Which of the following is suggestive of a ‘supportive’ technique?

options.text: Validation of the individual's emotional experience

questions.explanation: Dynamic (psychoanalytic) psychotherapy is often conceptualised as being on a continuum of expressive to supportive. Traditionally, psychoanalytic psychotherapy has focused on the recovery of repressed psychological material. This process has been called ‘expressive’ and is distinguished from the ‘supportive’ psychotherapies, which concentrate on supporting healthy defence (coping) mechanisms. The therapist may employ more or less expressive and supportive interventions, depending on the needs of the patient. Among the given responses in the question, advice giving leans towards the supportive end of the continuum. In addition to advice giving, other techniques usually employed that are at the supportive end of the continuum are praise, suggestions, reassurance, environmental intervention, and manipulation. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 928. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. (). Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2008, p. 1852.

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child shows strong resistance to parental direction regarding toileting, asserting control over when to pass stool. According to Freudian theory, which stage of development is this child likely in?
questions.explanation: The anal stage (18 months to 3 years) is specifically the period around potty training where the infant becomes able to control anal sphincter function and can decide when to pass stool. This sense of power and control is central to the anal stage. Fixation here may manifest as anally retentive personality traits or OCD-like controlling behaviors.

questions.question_text: The shadow, according to Jungian theory, represents which aspect of the psyche?

options.text: The collective inheritance of human symbolic material
The mask of personality presented to the outside world
A personification of the less acceptable aspects of oneself
The integration of masculine and feminine principles
The goals and aspirations one consciously pursues

correct_answer.text: A personification of the less acceptable aspects of oneself

questions.explanation: The shadow is specifically defined as a personification of the less acceptable aspects of oneself. The persona is the external mask. The collective unconscious contains inherited symbolic material. Individuation involves integrating all aspects including the shadow.

questions.question_text: What would be the average number of sessions in cognitive behavioral treatment?
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is usually a shortterm approach, typically with 12 to 20 sessions. CBT is a collaborative, structured, and goaloriented intervention that targets core components of a given disorder. The “cognitive” HIATRIC dISOR dERS • 85 element involves cognitive restructuring and problemsolving that addresses automatic thoughts. The “behavioral” component involves versions of monitoring, exposure, scheduling, and skills training.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach is most appropriate for alcohol addiction?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy (cue therapy) is a psychological treatment used to help individuals with substance use disorders reduce cravings and problematic behaviors by identifying and managing specific cues or triggers that lead to substance cravings and use. This is particularly effective for addiction.

questions.question_text: A patient is being treated for a severe phobia of needles. Teaching the patient relaxation strategies, while showing pictures of needles, working toward having them see an actual needle in the office, and then getting a shot at the doctor while experiencing minimal anxiety, is an example of which of the following types of therapies?
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization is the behavioral principle of counterconditioning, which helps the patient to overcome anxiety by gradually exposing them to the feared situation while they learn to be in a state that inhibits anxiety, called reciprocal inhibition.

questions.question_text: A patient in psychoanalytic therapy experiences an apparent slip of the tongue, saying I hope you fail your exams to their supportive therapist instead of I hope you pass your exams. According to Freudian theory, this parapraxis likely reflects which underlying process?

options.text: Poor auditory processing by the therapist
Return of repressed hostile or competitive feelings toward the therapist
Displacement of anxiety about the therapist's competence

correct_answer.text: Return of repressed hostile or competitive feelings toward the therapist

questions.explanation: This parapraxis (Freudian slip) is best understood as the return of repressed materials—in this case, possibly unconscious hostile or competitive feelings toward the therapist—slipping out as words. The slip reveals what is in the unconscious mind attempting to emerge. While displacement could occur, the direct nature of the hostile word suggests direct return of the repressed.

questions.question_text: A patient reports dreams in which a teacher and father figure appear merged into a single threatening character. Which dreamwork process best explains this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: This clinical example directly matches the definition of condensation: two or more unconscious impulses (feelings about strict father and punitive teacher) combined into a single image (frightening monster). Option A (diffusion) is the opposite process. Option C involves energy transfer. Option D uses innocent images. Option E is the overall dreamwork process.

questions.question_text: A therapist using psychodynamic principles asks a patient to free associate about childhood memories. According to Freudian theory, what is the primary therapeutic mechanism at work?

options.text: Strengthening the Ego's rational defenses against anxiety
Allowing repressed unconscious material to surface and become accessible
Teaching the patient to suppress unacceptable impulses
Creating new conscious memories to replace traumatic ones
Developing the Superego's capacity for moral judgment

correct_answer.text: Allowing repressed unconscious material to surface and become accessible

questions.explanation: Free association is explicitly described as helping to reveal aspects of the unconscious mind by encouraging patients to say whatever comes to mind. The therapeutic mechanism is accessing repressed material. It does not aim to strengthen defenses (option A), suppress impulses (option C), or create new memories (option D). It relates to unconscious material, not Superego development (option E).

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes symbolic representation in dreamwork?

options.text: The condensation of multiple symbols into one image
The displacement of emotion from one object to another
The use of an innocent or less highly charged image in place of something overwhelming
The transformation of latent into manifest dream content
The integration of day residues with unconscious impulses

correct_answer.text: The use of an innocent or less highly charged image in place of something overwhelming

questions.explanation: Symbolic representation is explicitly defined as using an innocent or less highly charged image in place of something that is potentially too overwhelming, exemplified by hunting a stag instead of murdering one's father. Option A describes condensation. Option B describes displacement. Option D is the overall process of dreamwork. Option E describes dream composition.

questions.question_text: A patient demonstrates rigidity, perfectionism, and excessive need for control in their personality. According to Freudian theory, this personality pattern might reflect fixation at which psychosexual stage?

options.text: Oral stage with fixation patterns of dependency
Anal stage with anally retentive character traits
Latency stage with suppression of sexuality

correct_answer.text: Anal stage with anally retentive character traits

questions.explanation: Anal stage fixation, particularly in the anally retentive direction, manifests as controlling personality traits, perfectionism, and the need for control. The source specifically states that anally retentive personality indicates controlling character. This can persist into disorders like OCD. The other stages do not specifically correlate with these traits.

questions.question_text: Justin is a medical student who faints every time he encounters medical situations involving blood or injury. His therapist trains him to tense the muscles of the arms, legs, and torso at the earliest signs of faintness. This type of treatment is called
questions.explanation: This is called applied tension. Unlike those with other specifi c phobias who show an increase in sympathetic output on exposure to phobic stimuli, patients with blood–injury– injection phobia show a unique, biphasic response. The fi rst phase is associated with increased heart rate and blood pressure. In the second phase, however, the blood pressure suddenly falls and the patient faints. To treat the problem, patients are shown a series of slides that are provocative (e.g. mutilated bodies). They are trained to identify early-warning signs of fainting, such as queasiness, cold sweats, or dizziness. They also learn how to apply the learned muscle tension response quickly, contingent on these warning signs. Patients can also perform applied tension while donating blood or watching a surgical operation. The technique of isometric tension raises blood pressure, which prevents fainting. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 952.

questions.question_text: Cue therapy is primarily used for treatment of which condition?
questions.explanation: Cue therapy is used to help individuals with alcohol addiction learn to manage responses to environmental cues that trigger addictive behaviors.

questions.question_text: According to Winnicott's theory, parental control and impositions can lead to development of which outcome?

options.text: Better reality testing and secondary process thinking
A false self different from the real self
Integration of good and bad object representations

correct_answer.text: A false self different from the real self

questions.explanation: Winnicott's theory specifically describes that parental control and impositions can lead to development of a false self different from the real self, representing his theory of multiple self organizations. This contrasts with healthy development where the true self can emerge and play in the transitional zone.

questions.question_text: In Freudian theory, the Oedipus complex in males is characterized by which of the following?

options.text: A wish to establish dominance over all male authority figures
A wish to kill the father and marry the mother
Rivalry with the mother for the father's affection
Fear of castration without aggressive impulses toward parents
Identification with the mother and rejection of masculine identity

correct_answer.text: A wish to kill the father and marry the mother

questions.explanation: The Oedipus complex is explicitly described as a wish to kill off the father to marry the mother. Option A is too general. Option C reverses the dynamics. Option D describes castration anxiety but not the complex itself. Option E describes atypical gender identification.

questions.question_text: A 4-year-old boy demonstrates possessiveness toward his mother and aggression toward his father. According to Freudian theory, this behavior is most consistent with which stage?
questions.explanation: The phallic/oedipal stage (3-5 years) is when genitals become of interest and differentiation occurs between boys and girls, stimulating oedipal feelings. The boy's wish to have the mother exclusively and competition with the father are hallmarks of this stage. Oral and anal stages precede it; latency follows.

questions.question_text: The Electra Complex, as described by Freud, involves which dynamic?

options.text: A daughter's wish to marry the mother and compete with the father
A girl's realization of not having a penis, feeling penis envy, and turning toward the father
Integration of masculine and feminine aspects of personality
Identification with the mother to develop maternal instincts
Regression to oral dependency on the mother

correct_answer.text: A girl's realization of not having a penis, feeling penis envy, and turning toward the father

questions.explanation: Freud described the Electra complex as girls realizing they and their mothers lack a penis, feeling penis envy, and turning toward the father (and later other men) to get a penis and have a baby. Freud acknowledged this thinking was heavily criticized and that he did not understand women well.

questions.question_text: Which psychological concept describes how an animal or person, when repeatedly exposed to an inescapable aversive stimulus, stops attempting to escape and develops passive, helpless behaviour?
questions.explanation: Learned helplessness (Seligman) is a psychological model  that describes how exposure to inescapable aversive stimuli leads animals and humans to stop attempting escape, exhibiting passive, helpless behaviour. It was originally proposed as a behavioural model for depression. In contrast, CBT, psychodynamic therapy, exposure therapy, and ACT are all actual therapeutic modalities. The stem\'s phrase \'form of therapy\' is therefore incompatible with learned helplessness as the correct answer.

questions.question_text: In Freudian theory, repression refers to which of the following processes?

options.text: Conscious suppression of unwanted memories through effort
Pushing unacceptable ideas, memories and thoughts out of awareness into the unconscious
The symbolic representation of unconscious wishes in dreams
The defence mechanism of projecting internal conflicts onto others
The integration of conflicting aspects of self during personality development

correct_answer.text: Pushing unacceptable ideas, memories and thoughts out of awareness into the unconscious

questions.explanation: Repression is explicitly defined as pushing unacceptable ideas, memories and thoughts out of awareness into the unconscious. Option A is incorrect because repression is unconscious, not a conscious effort. Option C refers to symbolic representation, which is part of dreamwork. Option D describes projection. Option E relates to integration processes in later developmental theories.

questions.question_text: In Jung's theory, the shadow is best described as which of the following?

options.text: The unconscious feminine aspects of the male psyche
A personification of the less acceptable aspects of oneself
The mask or persona presented to society
The collective inherited unconscious of all humanity
The integration of conscious and unconscious aspects of self

correct_answer.text: A personification of the less acceptable aspects of oneself

questions.explanation: The shadow is explicitly defined as a personification of the less acceptable aspects of oneself. Option A describes the anima. Option C describes the persona. Option D describes the collective unconscious. Option E describes individuation.

questions.question_text: Hypnotic suggestibility is associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Hypnotic suggestibility is associated with reduced metacognitive agency, meaning individuals have less robust awareness of how effectively they influence the world around them.

questions.question_text: Rachel is a 35-year-old woman who was recently involved in a life- threatening road traffi c accident. She developed symptoms suggestive of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) over a period of a month following the accident. The symptoms interfered with her daily activities. She refused to drive to work and started missing her work. She also stopped taking her children to the nursery. According to NICE guidelines, what treatment is recommended?

options.text: Monitoring of symptoms without active intervention for the first three months

questions.explanation: The NICE recommends ‘Watchful waiting’ when symptoms are mild and have been present for less than 4 weeks after the trauma, with a follow-up contact within 1 month. NICE specifi cally asks therapists and clinicians not to routinely offer brief, single-session interventions (debriefi ng) that focus on the traumatic incident to that individual alone. Where symptoms are present for less than 3 months (as in the case with Rachel), NICE specifi cally recommends trauma-focused CBT (usually on an individual outpatient basis. Trauma-focused CBT is also recommended for people with ‘severe’ symptoms or ‘severe’ PTSD within 1 month. NICE recommends 8–12 weekly sessions of trauma-focused CBT, each session delivered by the same person and lasting around 90 minutes during which trauma is discussed. NICE advises against the use of non-directed therapies such as relaxation training. Where symptoms are milder and have lasted for more than 3 months, NICE recommends either trauma-focused CBT or EMDR. In addition to psychological treatments, NICE also recommends specifi c pharmacological interventions. NICE. Clinical Guideline 26: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD): the management of PTSD in adults and children in primary and secondary care. www.nice.org.uk/CG026NICEguideline

questions.question_text: According to Erich Lindemann's stages of grief, which of the following is NOT a normal stage of grief?
questions.explanation: Lindemann described four stages of normal grief: shock (10-14 days), intense sadness with social withdrawal, anger/protest, and resolution within a year. Bargaining is part of Kübler-Ross's five-stage model (DABDA) but not Lindemann's original formulation. However, both models are recognized; the question may be testing Lindemann's specific model where bargaining is not explicitly included.

questions.question_text: Dialectical behavioural treatment uses all of the following techniques with the exception of
questions.explanation: Marsha Linehan developed dialectical therapy for patients with borderline personality disorder who repeatedly harm themselves. The treatment uses both behavioural and cognitive methods. It is highly structured and is manual based. Therapy is intense with individual sessions, skills training in a group and access by telephone to the therapist between sessions. It is delivered by a small team of therapists and lasts for up to a year. Individual sessions have four elements: cognitive behavioural techniques including self monitoring; dialectical ways of thinking about problems – seeing causality in terms of both/and rather than either/or and the possibility of reconciling opposites; mindfulness, that is the practice of detachment from the experience; use of aphorisms, that is phrases that encapsulate the approach –e.g. people may not have caused the problems, but have to solve them anyway. Skills training sessions are provided in a group basis and telephone contacts are designed to help patients get out of crises, by using the skills learnt in the sessions. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006p. 599.

questions.question_text: Individuation, in Jung's analytical psychology, refers to which developmental process?

options.text: The process in which an individual develops self-identity
Integration of the personal and collective unconscious

correct_answer.text: The process in which an individual develops self-identity

questions.explanation: Individuation is specifically defined as the process in which the individual develops self-identity. This is Jung's central concept of psychological development, involving integration of conscious and unconscious aspects including the persona, shadow, anima/animus, and self.

questions.question_text: Voucherbased contingency clinical approach has been found to have the best outcome in individuals with which of the following substance use disorders?

options.text: A diagnosis of cocaine use disorder
A diagnosis of alcohol use disorder
A diagnosis of cannabis use disorder
A diagnosis of tobacco use disorder
A diagnosis of opioid use disorder

correct_answer.text: A diagnosis of cocaine use disorder

questions.explanation: Several psychosocial therapies have been studied in cocaine use disorder, including 12step facilitation, 192 • PSYCHIATRY cognitive behavioral therapy, and contingency management. Voucherbased contingency management has yielded better outcomes in a number of studies in patients with cocaine use disorder. Patients with cocaine use disorder tend to score high on reward dependence, which is thought to mediate a portion of the effectiveness of contingency management. Re FeRe NCeS Budney, A. J., & Higgins, S. T. (1990). A community reinforcement plus vouchers approach: Treating cocaine addiction. Rockville, MD: National Institute on Drug Abuse. Petry, N. M., Tedford, J., Austin, M., Nich, C., Carroll, K. M., & Rounsaville, B. J. (2004). Prize reinforcement contingency management for treating cocaine users: How low can we go, and with whom? Addiction, 99, 349–

questions.question_text: Among the options below, which one psychotherapeutic modalities is most effective for substance use disorder?
questions.explanation: Although some of these psychotherapeutic modalities are used in patients with substance use disorders, the most effective modality is motivational interviewing. Re FeRe NCeS Miller, W. R., & Rollnick, S. (2012). Motivational interviewing: Helping people change. New York: Guilford Press. Work Group on Substance Use Disorders. (2006). American Psychiatric Association practice guideline for the treatment of patients with substance use disorders (2nd ed., p. 40). Retrieved from http:// psychiatryonline.org/ guidelines

questions.question_text: During substance abuse therapy, alcohol or substance signifier is used in controlled conditions. What therapy is this?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy involves presenting substance-related cues in controlled environments to reduce conditioned cravings and relapse.

questions.question_text: The manifest content of a dream, according to Freud, represents which aspect?

options.text: What the dreamer actually recalls upon waking
The symbolic representation of repressed material
The latent unconscious impulses before dream work

correct_answer.text: What the dreamer actually recalls upon waking

questions.explanation: Manifest content is specifically defined as what the dreamer recalls upon waking. Latent content comprises the unconscious thoughts, wishes, and conflicts. Dream work transforms latent content into manifest content through condensation, displacement, and symbolic representation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an alternative, effective treatment to dialectical behavioral therapy for severe borderline personality disorder?
questions.explanation: MBT is a psychotherapy developed for the treatment of borderline personality disorder. It focuses on the mentalizing vulnerabilities of the patient in helping them to understand the attachment process.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which forms of grief treatment treats unresolved grief as a form of phobic avoidance?
questions.explanation: Some individuals with abnormal grief reaction may be avoiding reminders of their grief, leading to unresolved emotions. Addressing these issues by encouragement may not be suffi cient and a behavioural approach may be needed in some cases. The approach commonly used is known as guided mourning. This treats unresolved grief in a way similar to other forms of phobic avoidance by exposure to the avoided situation. Thus guided mourning involves intense reliving of avoided painful memories and feelings associated with bereavement. During treatment, patients are exposed to avoided painful memories or situations related to the loss of their loved one – both in imagination and in real life. Clark A. Working with grieving adults. Advances in Psychiatric Treatment 2004; 10: 164–170.

questions.question_text: Which process in Freud's dream work involves energy invested in one object being transferred to another?
questions.explanation: Displacement is specifically defined as energy invested in one object or idea getting transferred to another (e.g., wishful fantasy about murdering father becomes shooting a teacher). Condensation combines impulses; symbolic representation uses innocent images; diffusion spreads one impulse across multiple images.

questions.question_text: What is the role the therapist should play in working with a patient for psychiatric rehabilitation?

options.text: To act as a parental figure
To be a shared decision maker
To make medical appointments for the patient
To suggest a variety of potential jobs for the patient
To take a stance on the patient not using alcohol or drugs

correct_answer.text: To be a shared decision maker

questions.explanation: The practitioner’s role is to be in a partnership with the patient to help improve their quality of life and collaborate with them and to work as a shared decision maker, rather than a parental or authority figure.

questions.question_text: What factor is known to increase the placebo effect?
questions.explanation: Injectable administration tends to enhance placebo effects compared to oral administration, likely due to increased ritual, expectation, and perceived potency associated with injections.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the preconscious according to Freud's Topographical Model?

options.text: The region containing repressed memories and impulses only
The interface between unconscious and conscious that maintains a repressive barrier
The region bound by time and space with secondary process thinking
The area containing the superego and ego functions
A reservoir of collective symbolic material

correct_answer.text: The interface between unconscious and conscious that maintains a repressive barrier

questions.explanation: The preconscious is specifically defined as being at the interface between unconscious and conscious, maintaining a repressive barrier that censors unacceptable wishes and desires. The unconscious contains repressed material; conscious is bound by time/space; the superego and ego are structural not topographical concepts.

questions.question_text: Habit reversal components include all the following with the exception of

options.text: Development of awareness of the behavior and its triggers
Practice of an incompatible alternative behavior

questions.explanation: Habit reversal is a complex procedure used generally to treat tics, Tourette’s syndrome and stuttering. The treatment has fi ve components – training in becoming aware of the onset of the behaviour; monitoring the behaviour; training in initiating competing responses that are compatible with the behaviour; relaxation; and social support. Training in thought stopping is not a component of habit reversal training. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006, p. 593.

questions.question_text: Which technique involves imagining and understanding the intentions, beliefs, and desires of others?
questions.explanation: Mentalization is the capacity to understand and imagine the intentions, beliefs, and desires of oneself and others, essential for social understanding and emotional regulation.

questions.question_text: According to Winnicott, the transitional object is best described as which of the following?

options.text: An imaginary companion created by children with attachment difficulties
An object invested with special meaning usually given by an important person but under the child's control
A defence mechanism protecting the child from separation anxiety
A symbolic representation of the mother in the child's unconscious
A fantasy figure that helps the child distinguish reality from imagination

correct_answer.text: An object invested with special meaning usually given by an important person but under the child's control

questions.explanation: The transitional object is explicitly defined as an object invested with special meaning usually given by an important person (like the mother) but which is under the child's control, exemplified by a teddy bear. Option A describes imaginary companions. Option C describes anxiety management but not the definition. Option D overstates the unconscious/symbolic nature. Option E mischaracterizes its function.

questions.question_text: The process by which unconscious ideas are repressed and prevented from reaching awareness because they are unacceptable in psychotherapy is called
questions.explanation: Resistance is broadly defined as the conscious or, more often, unconscious force within the patient opposing the emergence of unconscious material. Resistance is thought of as the patient’s attempt to protect her or himself by avoiding the anticipated emotional discomfort that accompanies the emergence of conflictual, dangerous, or painful experiences, feelings, thoughts, memories, needs, and desires. Resistance occurs through the use of unconscious defence mechanisms. The recognition, clarification, and interpretation of resistance constitute important activities of the psychoanalyst and the psychoanalytic psychotherapist, both of whom must first appreciate how a patient is warding off anxiety before understanding why he or she is so compelled. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 926.

questions.question_text: Dialectical behavioural treatment uses all of the following techniques with the exception of
questions.explanation: Marsha Linehan developed dialectical therapy for patients with borderline personality disorder who repeatedly harm themselves. The treatment uses both behavioural and cognitive methods. It is highly structured and is manual based. Therapy is intense with individual sessions, skills training in a group and access by telephone to the therapist between sessions. It is delivered by a small team of therapists and lasts for up to a year. Individual sessions have four elements: cognitive behavioural techniques including self monitoring; dialectical ways of thinking about problems – seeing causality in terms of both/and rather than either/or and the possibility of reconciling opposites; mindfulness, that is the practice of detachment from the experience; use of aphorisms, that is phrases that encapsulate the approach –e.g. people may not have caused the problems, but have to solve them anyway. Skills training sessions are provided in a group basis and telephone contacts are designed to help patients get out of crises, by using the skills learnt in the sessions. Gelder M, Harrison P, and Cowen P. Shorter Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry, 5th edn. Oxford University Press, 2006p. 599.

questions.question_text: A patient being treated for anxiety and depression tells the therapist about how embarrassed she was in forgetting the words for her class presentation today and states that she knows she will never make it as a teacher in the future. This is an example of which of the following cognitive distortions?
questions.explanation: Cognitive distortions, also known as automatic thoughts, are the thoughts that occur between external events and a person’s emotional reaction to the event. The vignette above is an example of overgeneralization in which an overwhelmingly negative conclusion is drawn from a relatively minor event.

questions.question_text: In Jungian theory, archetypes are best understood as which of the following?

options.text: Personal symbolic representations unique to each individual's history
Unconscious patterns resulting from individual life experiences
Representational images of universal symbolic meaning shared across cultures
Defensive mechanisms that protect the ego from anxiety
Learned behaviour patterns transmitted through social conditioning

correct_answer.text: Representational images of universal symbolic meaning shared across cultures

questions.explanation: Archetypes are defined as representational images of universal symbolic meaning (e.g., the Hero, the Old Wise Man). Option A describes personal complexes. Option B refers to individual unconscious content. Option D relates to defence mechanisms. Option E describes learned behaviours outside Jungian theory.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man with a history of obsessive-compulsive features reports difficulty with emotional expression and excessive need for order and control in his environment. Based on psychoanalytic theory, which psychosexual stage fixation would this presentation most suggest?
questions.explanation: The combination of control needs and OCD-like features directly matches anal stage fixation characteristics, where the power of controlling anal sphincter function becomes a template for personality organization. The patient's age and chronicity support fixation at this developmental level. Option A would present with dependency and oral concerns. Option C involves repression of sexuality. Option D involves identity and competitive issues. Option E represents mature functioning.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the anima in Jungian psychology?

options.text: The conscious aspect of an individual's personality
The unconscious feminine aspect of a man
The mask one presents to the outside world
The collective symbolic past of mankind
The set of ideas and feelings triggered by interpersonal interactions

correct_answer.text: The unconscious feminine aspect of a man

questions.explanation: The anima is explicitly defined as the unconscious feminine aspect of a man. Option A describes the ego. Option C describes the persona. Option D describes the collective unconscious. Option E describes complexes in the personal unconscious.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which in the least likely outcome in a individual undergoing CBT for hypochondriasis?

options.text: Less distress at thoughts of illness
A diagnosis of decrease in health-related anxiety

questions.explanation: In a 12-month follow-up randomized controlled trial of CBT vs treatment as usual, CBT was found to be better than medical care as usual. Compared with the control group, the CBT group had signifi cantly lower levels of hypochondriacal symptoms, beliefs, and attitudes and health-related anxiety at 12 months. They also had less impairment of social role functioning and intermediate activities of daily living. However, hypochondriacal somatic symptoms did not improve signifi cantly. The authors of the study Barsky and Ahern explained, ‘Conceptually, hypochondriacal somatic symptoms cannot simply be stripped away with symptomatic treatment, because they exist for underlying psychological and interpersonal reasons. This suggests that a realistic goal in treating hypochondriasis is amelioration of distressing fears and beliefs and improved coping, rather than the elimination of somatic symptoms per se.’ Barsky AJ and Ahern DK. Cognitive behavior therapy for hypochondriasis: a randomized, controlled trial. Journal of the American Medical Association 2004; 291: 1464–1470.

questions.question_text: In Freudian theory, the superego is best characterized as which of the following?

options.text: The instinctual part of personality expressing sexual and aggressive impulses
The seat of internalised morals, values, and conscience
The mediating structure that balances instinct and reality
The unconscious repository of repressed memories
The defensive mechanism that protects against anxiety

correct_answer.text: The seat of internalised morals, values, and conscience

questions.explanation: The superego is explicitly described as the seat of internalised morals and values, functioning as conscience. It can be punishing or helpful in striving for goals (Ego Ideal). Option A describes the id. Option C describes the ego. Option D describes the unconscious. Option E describes defence mechanisms.

questions.question_text: An alcoholic patient is taken to a place with alcohol and environmental cues associated with drinking, but prevented from drinking. What therapeutic technique is this?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy involves exposing the patient to cues associated with substance use while preventing the use, with the goal of extinguishing the conditioned craving response.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which correctly describes counter-transference?

options.text: The analyst’s or psychotherapist’s transference reactions to the individual
His or her reactions to the individual’s transferences
Any reactions, feelings and attitudes of the analyst or therapist towards the individual, regardless of their source.

questions.explanation: Freud used the term counter-transference to describe the analyst’s transference towards the patient. In other words, the patient might remind the therapist of someone from the therapist’s past, so that the therapist starts to treat the patient as though he or she were that fi gure. Over time, this view of counter-transference was broadened to include the total emotional reaction of the therapist to the patient. Today it is recognized that counter- transference is jointly created—it partly involves the therapist’s past relationships, but it also involves feelings induced in the therapist by the patient’s behaviour. Counter-transference is variously defi ned as (1) the analyst’s or psychotherapist’s transference reactions to the patient; (2) his or her reactions to the patient’s transferences; and (3) any reactions, feelings and attitudes of the analyst or therapist toward the patient, regardless of their source. These responses are manifestations of the requisite engagement by the therapist or analyst in the emotional process of treatment. Moreover, these reactions are a rich source of understanding of the patient’s experience as it touches the therapist affectively. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 58. Tasman A, Maj M, First MB, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2008, p. 1854.

questions.question_text: Which intervention specifically focuses on enabling the patient to express personal reasons for and against improving their treatment adherence?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing enables the patient to express personal reasons for and against improving their treatment adherence.

questions.question_text: Among the following options, which is an evidencebased treatment for PTSD?
questions.explanation: Cognitive Processing Therapy and Prolonged Exposure Therapy are evidencebased psychotherapy treatments for PTSD. Cognitive Processing Therapy involves written accounts of the trauma narrative with cognitive restructuring. In Prolonged Exposure Therapy, the trauma narrative is repeated orally during the therapy, and in vivo exposures are utilized to reduce distress and avoid situations impacted by the PTSD. Fluoxetine is an SSRI antidepressant that is used to reduce symptoms of PTSD. Each of these three treatments can help PTSD symptoms related to reexperiencing (such as nightmares), avoidance (such as detachment), and hyperarousal (such as hypervigilance).

questions.question_text: Which of the following concepts in Freudian theory explains how unconscious material can be accessed during therapy?

options.text: The reality principle governing the conscious mind
The return of the repressed materials through parapraxes and dreams
The strengthening of secondary process thinking
The expansion of ego capacity for rational thought

correct_answer.text: The return of the repressed materials through parapraxes and dreams

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that parapraxes and dreams give clues to unconscious material and are due to the return of the repressed. This is the fundamental mechanism by which unconscious content becomes accessible. Option A describes conscious functioning. Option C relates to ego development. Option D is not a therapeutic mechanism. Option E is a treatment goal but not how content is accessed.

questions.question_text: What is the primary modality of social skills training?
questions.explanation: Social skills rehabilitation can help improve social perceptions, social cognitions, and behavioral responses via focusing on role-playing of simulated conversations.

questions.question_text: In family systems theory, what is the term for being aware that people's interactions are influenced by each other, which in turn are influenced by others?
questions.explanation: Circular causality describes a sequence of causes and effects that leads back to the original cause and either alters or confirms it, producing a new sequence like a feedback loop. This reflects the systemic understanding that interactions are mutually influential.

questions.question_text: According to psychoanalytic theory, the preconscious mind functions primarily to maintain which psychological process?

options.text: Repression of instinctual impulses through censoring
Integration of conscious and unconscious material

correct_answer.text: Repression of instinctual impulses through censoring

questions.explanation: The preconscious is specifically described as maintaining a repressive barrier that censors unacceptable wishes and desires. It functions at the interface between unconscious and conscious, filtering what can reach consciousness. The unconscious operates via pleasure principle; the conscious via reality-testing.

questions.question_text: Which concept in Jung's analytical psychology refers to the unconscious feminine aspect within men?
questions.explanation: The anima is specifically defined as the unconscious feminine aspect of a man. The animus is the unconscious masculine aspect of a woman (the opposite). The persona is the external mask. The shadow represents less acceptable aspects. The collective unconscious is mankind's symbolic past.

questions.question_text: Which intervention primarily targets a patient's attitudes and beliefs to influence the personal construction of the meaning of illness?
questions.explanation: Cognitive-based interventions target the patient’s attitudes and beliefs towards medication to influence the personal construction of the meaning of medication and illness.

questions.question_text: According to Freudian psychosexual theory, a fixation at the anal stage in adulthood may manifest as which of the following?

options.text: Excessive dependence on others and alcoholism
Inability to form stable identity and diffused goals
Difficulty with authority figures and rebellious behaviour

questions.explanation: Anal stage fixation is explicitly described as potentially manifesting in controlling character traits and disorders such as OCD, reflecting the power and control theme of potty training. Option A relates to oral fixation. Option B relates to phallic fixation. Option D relates to identity formation. Option E relates to Oedipal conflicts.

questions.question_text: During her fi rst session, Lisa asks her therapist about certain terms she came across on the internet. “What is transference?”

options.text: A learned response pattern that the individual applies to the therapist
Therapist’s response to the individual based on the therapist’s previous relationships
individual’s response to the therapist based on the individual’s previous relationships
Transfer of positive thoughts from the therapist to the individual through self-disclosure

correct_answer.text: individual’s response to the therapist based on the individual’s previous relationships

questions.explanation: Transference is the displacement of feelings and thoughts associated with a fi gure in the patient’s past onto the therapist. Transference is often unconscious, at least initially, and the patient is often puzzled by their behaviour towards the therapist because it does not make sense, based on who the therapist really is. Hence the enactment of missing a session or of coming late to a session may reveal unconscious transference. The prevailing view about transference is that the therapist’s actual behaviour always infl uences the patient’s experience of the therapist. Hence the transference to the therapist is partly based on real characteristics and partly on fi gures from the patient’s past: a combination of old and new relationships. Many therapists believe that interpretation of this transference is an essential process of psychodynamic psychotherapy. Gabbard says that one should postpone the interpretation of transference until it becomes a resistance and until it is close to the patient’s awareness. In other words, if things are going reasonably well, it makes no sense to interpret transference. If the patient develops, for example, erotized or highly negative feelings, which impede the process of the therapy, interpretation may be essential. Many therapists regard treatment that focuses on transference as more exploratory than therapy geared to extra-transference relationships. In supportive therapy, interpretation of the transference may be minimized, although the therapist may silently interpret the transference as a way of increasing his or her understanding of the patient. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 56. Tasman A, Maj M, First M B, et al. Psychiatry, 3rd edn. WileyBlackwell, 2008, p. 1854.

questions.question_text: In Jungian psychology, complexes are best understood as which of the following?

options.text: Unconscious conflicts stemming from repressed desires
Sets of ideas and feelings triggered by interpersonal interactions
Archetypal patterns shared across all human cultures
Defence mechanisms protecting the ego from anxiety
Developmental fixations from unresolved childhood stages

correct_answer.text: Sets of ideas and feelings triggered by interpersonal interactions

questions.explanation: Complexes in Jungian theory are explicitly defined as sets of ideas and feelings triggered by interpersonal interactions, located in the personal unconscious. Option A describes Freudian conflicts. Option C describes archetypes. Option D describes defence mechanisms. Option E describes psychosexual fixations.

questions.question_text: In Freud's psychosexual development theory, which stage is characterized by the infant's focus on the mouth and sucking?
questions.explanation: The oral stage (0 to 18 months) is explicitly defined as the period where the mouth and sucking are the infant's focus. Option A (18 months to 3 years) involves potty training. Option C (3-5 years) involves genital differentiation. Options B and E occur at different developmental periods.

questions.question_text: In family systems theory, what term describes family members ganging up against one family member?
questions.explanation: Detouring occurs when parents form an alliance against the child, creating scapegoating. This functions to create distance between the parents themselves while increasing closeness in their own relationship, and parents direct negativity toward the child rather than addressing marital tension.

questions.question_text: During substance abuse treatment, people believe they are helpless, hopeless, and powerless. What program is this?
questions.explanation: The 12-step program emphasizes acceptance of powerlessness and the need for a higher power in recovery from addiction.

questions.question_text: The distinction between manifest and latent dream content is that manifest content represents which of the following in relation to latent content?

options.text: The unconscious wishes and repressed thoughts
What the dreamer recalls and reports upon waking
The condensed and displaced symbolic material
The residual sensations from sleep stimuli
The integration of day's experiences with instinctual impulses

correct_answer.text: What the dreamer recalls and reports upon waking

questions.explanation: Manifest content is explicitly defined as what the dreamer recalls, while latent content comprises unconscious thoughts and wishes. Dreamwork transforms latent into manifest. Option A describes latent content. Option C describes the dreamwork process. Option D describes dream composition elements. Option E describes dream formation but not the manifest-latent distinction.

questions.question_text: Which statement about transference is correct?
questions.explanation: Transference can be psychotic, involving severe distortions of therapist's identity and role.

questions.question_text: What is the term for the ability to maintain moment-by-moment awareness of thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations, and environment?
questions.explanation: Mindfulness means maintaining a moment-by-moment awareness of our thoughts, feelings, bodily sensations, and surrounding environment through a gentle, nurturing lens.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which statements accurately describes collaborative empiricism in CBT?

options.text: A relationship where the therapist validates the client's beliefs without questioning them
A relationship in which the treatment is considered empirical with no guaranteed positive outcome in order to avoid later disappointment
A relationship in which the therapist discloses personal problems to the client for mutual problem-solving
A relationship in which the therapist and the client work as partners in identifying and modifying dysfunctional cognitions and behaviours.
A relationship in which the client agrees for the therapist to share information with multiple other therapists who offer different models of treatment

correct_answer.text: A relationship in which the therapist and the client work as partners in identifying and modifying dysfunctional cognitions and behaviours.

questions.explanation: Collaborative empiricism is a term used in cognitive therapy to describe the therapeutic relationship with a high degree of collaboration and an experimental but pragmatic tone to the therapy. This allows the therapist to formulate hypotheses and helps the client to test the validity of the hypotheses, thus actively contributing to the client’s therapy. It does not necessarily mean that the client and the therapist must agree with each other on every aspect of the therapy. In addition, the therapist need not collude with dysfunctional assumptions the client holds in order to achieve the collaboration. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 964.

questions.question_text: Condensation in dreamwork involves which of the following?

options.text: One unconscious impulse represented by several images
Two or more unconscious impulses combined into a single image
Energy invested in one idea transferred to another
An innocent image substituted for an overwhelming fantasy
The transformation of manifest content into latent content

correct_answer.text: Two or more unconscious impulses combined into a single image

questions.explanation: Condensation is explicitly defined as two or more unconscious impulses being combined into a single image, exemplified by a strict father and punitive teacher combining into one frightening monster. Option A describes diffusion/irradiation. Option C describes displacement. Option D describes symbolic representation. Option E reverses the direction of dreamwork.

questions.question_text: Which scenario would make a patient a good candidate for psychoanalysis?

options.text: A diagnosis of a new medical condition
Possessing an urgent need for symptom relief

questions.explanation: Good candidates for psychoanalysis must truly wish to understand themselves and not need urgent symptom relief. Being able to withstand frustration and anxiety without acting out are important characteristics to possess in order for psychoanalysis to be successful.

questions.question_text: Cognitive behavioural therapy using exposure techniques may work by facilitating fear extinction through which mechanism?

options.text: Blocking NMDA receptor activation during exposure to prevent re-conditioning
Increasing serotonergic tone in the amygdala via stress-induced neuroplasticity
Requiring the patient to confront feared stimuli in a safe environment, triggering extinction learning in the amygdala
Reducing noradrenergic output from the locus coeruleus through relaxation training
Strengthening VMPFC-to-thalamus connectivity, bypassing the amygdala entirely

correct_answer.text: Requiring the patient to confront feared stimuli in a safe environment, triggering extinction learning in the amygdala

questions.explanation: Exposure-based CBT is hypothetically effective because it confronts patients with feared stimuli in a safe therapeutic environment without adverse consequences. Repeated safe exposure triggers the process of fear extinction in the amygdala — the VMPFC and hippocampus learn a new, safe context for the feared stimulus and establish new inhibitory connections in the amygdala. The limitation is that this learning is often context-specific, explaining why benefits may not fully generalise to real-world environments.

questions.question_text: In Freud's model of mind, primary process thinking is characterized by which of the following?

options.text: Logical reasoning bound by time and space
Thinking that defies logic and is not restricted by reality
The application of learned social rules and conventions
The synthesis of emotional and rational thought

correct_answer.text: Thinking that defies logic and is not restricted by reality

questions.explanation: Primary process thinking is explicitly described as defying logic and not being restricted by reality, characteristic of the unconscious mind. Option A describes secondary process thinking. Option B describes conscious thought. Option D describes superego-influenced thinking. Option E describes integrated functioning.

questions.question_text: In Freud's conceptualization, instincts create pressure by seeking fulfillment, and this pressure leads directly to which experience?
questions.explanation: Freud specifically stated that the pressure arising from instincts pressing to be fulfilled leads to anxiety. The mind developed to manage these instincts and their associated pressures. Anxiety serves as a signal that motivates defense mechanisms and adaptation.

questions.question_text: Group therapy would be contraindicated for a patient in which of the following scenarios?

options.text: A new diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia with active delusions
A patient actively engaged in individual therapy, suffering from depression and suicidal thoughts
Bipolar disorder with manic symptoms has been diagnosed, though the patient is stable on medications
The patient has antisocial personality disorder and is with others in the group with the same diagnosis
The patient is suffering from an acute grief reaction after the death of a spouse

correct_answer.text: A new diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia with active delusions

questions.explanation: There are relatively few contraindications to participating in group therapy. A patient with active delusions, who incorporate the group into the delusions, and a patient who is threatening with frequent outbursts are some examples of patients who should be excluded from the group setting.

questions.question_text: According to Freud, the resolution of the Oedipus Complex leads directly to which developmental outcome?

options.text: Formation of the Superego with introjection of parental values
Integration of the shadow and persona

correct_answer.text: Formation of the Superego with introjection of parental values

questions.explanation: Freud explicitly stated that resolution of the Oedipus Complex leads to formation of the Superego through introjection of parental values, specifically the prohibition of patricide and incest. This is the critical developmental milestone of the phallic stage.

questions.question_text: A key limitation of exposure-based CBT is that:

options.text: It is only effective in patients without comorbid depression
It only applies to phobic avoidance and not to anticipatory anxiety or worry
It requires a minimum of 24 weeks to produce measurable amygdala changes on neuroimaging
Therapeutic benefit is often context-specific, as the hippocampus encodes the context of extinction, and fear may be renewed in the real world
It is dependent on concurrent SSRI administration to generalise across contexts

correct_answer.text: Therapeutic benefit is often context-specific, as the hippocampus encodes the context of extinction, and fear may be renewed in the real world

questions.explanation: Because the hippocampus stores the contextual information of where extinction occurred, the therapeutic learning may be restricted to the specific context in which it was acquired — typically the therapist's office. Outside that context, in environments associated with the original trauma or fear, the original conditioning may reassert itself (renewal). Current psychotherapy research is investigating how to use contextual cues to strengthen generalisation of extinction learning across different environments.

questions.question_text: The therapeutic work of interpersonal psychotherapy is organized around central interpersonal problem areas in the individual’s life. Which of the following situations are possible problem areas in a case of acute depression?
questions.explanation: In acute treatment for depression with IPT, the problem areas can be classifi ed as role transitions (associated with stressful life events), grief, role disputes (e.g. in marriage), or interpersonal defi cits (lack of social support). Although specifi c stressful experiences are relevant to other IPT problem areas in the broadest sense, adjusting to stress and change in the social context requires a role transition. This might be the case in depression following the birth of a child, retirement, medical illness, divorce, etc. According to IPT, bereavement is thought to be a potential precursor of clinical depression. Development of clinical depression following a death is evidence that the normal grief process did not take place and that the individual has had an abnormal grief reaction. In such cases the work of IPT is to help the patient experience the normal grief process. A role dispute can occur in any important relationship especially the patient’s relationship with his or her spouse or signifi cant other. In interpersonal defi cits, the patient’s primary problem is seen as a paucity of social connections. Relationships buffer the individual against stressful life events and are essential to psychological well-being. As such, the primary goal is to enhance the level of social connection through concrete positive changes in the patient’s social activities (e.g. joining a club, taking a class). Attention to social support and a positive social network is also a component of work in the other IPT problem areas. Gabbard GO. Textbook of Psychotherapeutic Treatments in Psychiatry, 1st edn. American Psychiatric Publishing, 2008, p. 275.

questions.question_text: A woman reports a dream in which she is hunting a stag, which she associates with her unconscious wish to harm her father. This dream imagery best exemplifies which dream work mechanism?

options.text: Symbolic representation using an innocent image
Diffusion of aggression across multiple targets

correct_answer.text: Symbolic representation using an innocent image

questions.explanation: This exemplifies symbolic representation, where an innocent or less highly charged image (hunting a stag) is used in place of something potentially overwhelming (harming the father). The stag substitutes for the father figure. The source specifically gives this example of how a wishful fantasy about shooting one's father becomes the image of hunting a stag.

questions.question_text: Among the following, which indicates suffi cient psychological mindedness in Lisa?

options.text: She is capable of describing her feelings without excessive defensive reactions
She demonstrates insight into the connections between past experiences and current patterns
She recognizes the influence of unconscious motivations on her behavior
She does not have poor self-esteem
She can engage in self-reflection and examine her own mental processes

correct_answer.text: She does not have poor self-esteem

questions.explanation: According to Nina Coltart, during psychotherapy, a therapist is exercising his/her skills and psychological mindedness to explore the patient’s psyche. If the patient is also psychologically minded, the prospects of treatment success are thought to be greatly increased. Whether a patient is psychologically minded depends on a number of characters. They include: 1. The capacity to give a history that deepens, acquires more coherence, and becomes texturally more substantial as it goes on. 2. The capacity to give such a history without needing too much prompting, and a history which gives the listener an increasing awareness that the patient feels currently related in him/herself, to his/her own story. 3. The capacity to bring up memories with appropriate affects. 4. Some awareness in the patient that he has an unconscious mental life. 5. Some capacity to step back, if only momentarily, from self-experience, and to observe it refl ectively. 6. The capacity, or more strongly a wish, to accept and handle increased responsibility for the self. 7. The capacity to imagine and dream and use metaphors. 8. Some capacity for achievement, and some realistic self-esteem. Coltart N. The assessment of psychological-mindedness in the diagnostic interview. British Journal of Psychiatry 1988; 153: 819–820. Naismith J and Grant S. Seminars in the Psychotherapies. Gaskell, 2007, p. 8.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old patient entering psychodynamic therapy has significant difficulty forming close relationships and frequently speaks of feeling isolated and watched by others. Which Jungian concept best relates to these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The patient's difficulty with relationships and feeling watched, combined with isolation, suggests introversion and inadequate individuation (development of self-identity). This is a 2-step inference requiring linking interpersonal isolation with Jungian developmental concepts. Option A (persona) involves presentation to world but not isolation. Option B (anima) is specific to male-female dynamics. Option C (shadow) involves disowned aspects but not specifically isolation. Option E is too broad/non-specific.

questions.question_text: Free association in psychodynamic therapy is primarily used to accomplish which of the following?

options.text: To teach the patient rational thought processes
To encourage the patient to say whatever comes to mind, revealing aspects of the unconscious
To practice social skills and interpersonal communication
To replace maladaptive thought patterns with adaptive ones
To establish a collaborative therapeutic relationship

correct_answer.text: To encourage the patient to say whatever comes to mind, revealing aspects of the unconscious

questions.explanation: Free association is explicitly described as encouraging the patient to say whatever comes into his mind, however fleeting or trivial, to reveal aspects of the unconscious mind. Option A relates to cognitive approaches. Option C describes social skills training. Option D describes cognitive therapy. Option E is a general therapeutic goal.

questions.question_text: A patient reports that in a recent dream, both their strict father and a punitive teacher appeared as a single frightening monster. This dream imagery best illustrates which dream work process?
questions.explanation: This is a classic example of condensation, where two or more unconscious impulses are combined into a single image (the strict father and punitive teacher becoming one monster). Displacement would transfer energy to a different object. Symbolic representation uses innocent images. Diffusion spreads one impulse across multiple images.

questions.question_text: Secondary Process thinking, as described in Freud's Topographical Model, is characterized by which feature?

options.text: Defiance of logic and freedom from reality constraints
Being bound by time and space with logical reasoning
Unconscious wish fulfillment and pleasure seeking

correct_answer.text: Being bound by time and space with logical reasoning

questions.explanation: Secondary Process thinking is specifically characterized as being bound by time and space, linked to reality and conscious processing. Primary Process thinking defies logic and is not restricted by reality. Secondary process is the rational, reality-based mode of the conscious mind.

questions.question_text: Dawn is known to have moderate learning disability. She hits her head very often with her right hand. Her therapist teaches Dawn to engage in knitting with her right hand. This gradually replaced her maladaptive behaviour. The process through which the therapist replaced a maladaptive behaviour with an adaptive constructive one is through the principles of

options.text: Systematic reinforcement of alternative adaptive behaviors incompatible with the target behavior

questions.explanation: Positive behavioural programming was developed to concentrate solely on interventions designed to increase desired behaviours with the theoretical argument that these would then replace problem behaviours. In this case there has been differential reinforcement of a more positive activity. Functional communication training is an example of positive behaviour programming. It is based on the hypothesis that problem behaviours are usually communication needs. Individuals are taught to communicate through alternative more acceptable ways. Freeman C and Power M. Handbook of Evidence-based Psychotherapies: A Guide for Research and Practice, 1st edn. WileyBlackwell, 2007, p. 199.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic technique combines Rogerian client-centered therapy with Beck's cognitive behavioral therapy?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing integrates Rogerian person-centered techniques with cognitive-behavioral principles to enhance intrinsic motivation for change.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes a Freudian slip (parapraxis)?

options.text: A deliberate withholding of information during psychotherapy
An unconscious verbal error revealing repressed material that slips out during conversation
A memory distortion caused by the passage of time
A defensive avoidance of discussing emotionally charged topics
A symptom of poor concentration or attention deficit

correct_answer.text: An unconscious verbal error revealing repressed material that slips out during conversation

questions.explanation: Parapraxes are explicitly described as Freudian slips where repressed materials slip out as words during conversation due to the return of the repressed. Option A describes conscious withholding, not a slip. Option C refers to memory distortion without the psychodynamic mechanism. Option D describes avoidance rather than an involuntary slip. Option E incorrectly attributes it to attention problems.

questions.question_text: Which therapeutic approach involves reflecting on how intended outcomes are affected by current behaviors?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing is a counseling method that helps people resolve ambivalent feelings and insecurities to find internal motivation for behavior change, considering the difficulty of making life changes. It involves reflecting on discrepancies between current behaviors and desired outcomes. While Rogerian therapy uses reflection, motivational interviewing specifically focuses on exploring the gap between current behavior and intended outcomes.

questions.question_text: During substance abuse therapy, the use of alcohol or substance signifier in controlled conditions is characteristic of which therapy?
questions.explanation: Cue exposure therapy is a behavioral therapy technique where alcohol or substance cues are presented in controlled conditions to reduce conditioned responses and craving.

questions.question_text: According to Freud's theory of dreams, which component includes unconscious thoughts, wishes, and the residues from daily experience?
questions.explanation: Latent content is specifically defined as comprising unconscious mental matter (thoughts, wishes), residues from the day, and stimuli experienced during sleep. Manifest content is what is recalled. Dream work is the process transforming latent into manifest. Evidence shows this exact definition in the diagram.

questions.question_text: Which intervention specifically uses analogies with chronic physical illness to explore the pros and cons of medication?
questions.explanation: In compliance therapy, a patient’s ambivalence towards medication is explored, analogies with chronic physical illness are made, and the pros and cons of medication are considered during the course of treatment.

questions.question_text: Which aspect of Freud's theory proposes that the mind developed primarily to manage instincts and their associated pressures?

options.text: The instinct theory and the pressure they create
The structural model of id, ego, and superego

correct_answer.text: The instinct theory and the pressure they create

questions.explanation: Freud maintained that the mind developed in order to manage instincts, with the pressure arising from instincts pressing to be fulfilled leading to anxiety. This is the foundational premise of instinct theory explaining psychological development and functioning. The structural model (id, ego, superego) is his mechanism for explaining how the mind manages instincts.

questions.question_text: In Freud's topographical model, the preconscious is best characterized as which of the following?

options.text: The region containing only repressed memories and instinctual impulses
The interface between the unconscious and conscious, maintaining a repressive barrier
The part of the mind linked with external reality and logical thought
The seat of internalised moral values and the superego
The zone where fantasy and reality become indistinguishable

correct_answer.text: The interface between the unconscious and conscious, maintaining a repressive barrier

questions.explanation: The preconscious is defined as being at the interface between the unconscious and conscious, maintaining a repressive barrier that censors unacceptable wishes. Option A describes the unconscious. Option C describes the conscious mind. Option D refers to the superego in the structural model. Option E relates to Winnicott's transitional zone.

questions.question_text: A method of group psychotherapy where members of the group take on the roles of ‘the protagonist’ and ‘auxillary ego’ while the therapist takes on the role of ‘the director’ is
questions.explanation: Psychodrama is a method of group psychotherapy originated by Jacob Moreno, a Viennese-born psychiatrist. In this type of psychotherapy, the personality make-up, interpersonal relationships, confl icts, and emotional problems are explored by means of special ‘dramatic’ methods. Therapeutic dramatization of emotional problems includes the ‘protagonist’ or patient, the person who acts out his/her problems. The enactment is carried out with the help of ‘auxiliary egos’, people who enact varying aspects of the patient. The therapist takes up the role of the ‘director’ and guides those in the drama towards the acquisition of insight. Situations are chosen by the protagonist – this usually focuses on any special area of functioning or symptoms. The auxiliary ego takes on the role of other signifi cant people in the protagonist’s life. The therapist directs the situations, and the group can comment on various ways in which the protagonist deals with the situation he/she is in. Techniques to advance the therapeutic process and to increase productivity and creativity include the soliloquy (a recital of overt and hidden thoughts and feelings), role reversal (the exchange of the patient’s role for the role of a signifi cant person), the double (an auxiliary ego acting as the patient), the multiple double (several egos acting as the patient did on varying occasions), and the mirror technique (an ego imitating the patient and speaking for him or her). Other techniques include the use of hypnosis and psychoactive drugs to modify the acting behaviour in various ways. Sadock BJ and Sadock VA. Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry: Behavioral Sciences/clinical Psychiatry, 10th edn. Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, 2007, p. 939.

questions.question_text: In Freud's structural model, which component is primarily unconscious and contains sexual and aggressive impulses?
questions.explanation: The id is specifically defined as full of instinctual aspects including sexual and aggressive impulses, and is mostly unconscious. The ego is the executive linked to reality. The superego contains internalized morals. Persona and anima are Jungian concepts.

questions.question_text: Melanie Klein's paranoid-schizoid position involves which of the following features?
